title: Token-Balanced Continual Pretraining Eliminates Brain Rot Degradation

contributions.purpose: Reframe the cause of 'Brain Rot' degradation during continual pretraining (CPT) on short-sequence data.
contributions.mechanism: Controlled experiments attributing Brain Rot to per-token weight disparity (short sequences receive disproportionately high per-token gradient updates) rather than to low-quality semantic content.
contributions.evaluation: Measures an 8.17x per-token gradient/weight disparity in their experiments as the causal mechanism.
contributions.domain: Continual pretraining of large language models on short-sequence corpora.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that Brain Rot is a training artifact caused by per-token weight disparity (8.17x in our experiments), not an inherent property of low-quality semantic content.

contributions.purpose: Eliminate Brain Rot degradation via a training procedure fix.
contributions.mechanism: Token-balanced packing concatenates multiple short sequences to uniform length, equalizing per-token gradient contributions.
contributions.evaluation: On Llama-3-8B-Instruct achieves 119.7% ARC reasoning recovery and 95.2% RULER long-context recovery relative to the no-CPT baseline.
contributions.domain: Continual pretraining of large language models on short-sequence corpora.
contributions.source_quote: We show that token-balanced packing achieves full capability recovery, with 119.7% ARC reasoning recovery and 95.2% RULER long-context recovery relative to the no-CPT baseline.

contributions.mechanism: Mechanistic analysis showing packing equalizes gradient contributions across sequences, removing per-token weight disparity.
contributions.evaluation: Analysis links removal of the 8.17x disparity to eliminated degradation (qualitative mechanistic evidence).
contributions.domain: Continual pretraining of large language models on short-sequence corpora.
contributions.source_quote: We provide mechanistic analysis showing that packing eliminates per-token weight disparity by equalizing gradient contributions across sequences.

contributions.purpose: Show the efficiency benefit of packing.
contributions.mechanism: Compares packed vs unpacked CPT training wall-clock/throughput.
contributions.evaluation: Packing provides a 67x training speedup compared to unpacked training.
contributions.domain: Continual pretraining of large language models on short-sequence corpora.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that packing provides a 67x training speedup compared to unpacked training, making it both more effective and more efficient.

self_declared_provenance.quote: Most relevant to our work, Xing et al. (2025) identified the 'Brain Rot' phenomenon where CPT on short social media posts severely degrades model capabilities, attributing this to low-quality semantic content. Our work challenges this attribution by demonstrating that the degradation stems from training dynamics rather than content quality.

The prevailing explanation for Brain Rot attributes the degradation to the semantic quality of the training data itself... However, we hypothesize that Brain Rot is not an inherent property of low-quality content, but rather a training artifact arising from how standard training procedures handle variable-length sequences.
